terms.meaning: The fighters themselves — mostly Basic Pokémon plus Stage 1 and Stage 2 Evolution cards; the corner of the card shows its stage and, for Evolutions, what it evolves from.
Fuel most attacks need; a printed cost symbol must be matched by the right Energy type, except for costs that accept any type.
Items, Supporters, Stadiums, and Pokémon Tools; the corner names the specific subtype, with any special rule for that subtype printed at the bottom.

state: All four pieces share one card name, so the deck-building copy cap counts them together as that one name rather than four separate names
Every copy of the same Pokémon V-UNION name in a deck must come from the same set and share the same illustrator
All four pieces must be played to the Bench in a single motion, straight from the discard pile — playing only part of the set isn't allowed
Occupies just one Bench spot and can hold only a single Pokémon Tool at a time
Each distinct Pokémon V-UNION name can be played at most once per game, though a different V-UNION name may still be played afterward
Is not a Basic Pokémon, so it cannot start the game as the Active Pokémon or a Benched Pokémon during setup
A deck built only from Pokémon V-UNION still needs at least one ordinary Basic Pokémon
Is not an Evolution card and instead occupies its own unique stage
Card effects keyed to "Basic," "Stage 1," "Stage 2," or "Evolution" skip over it entirely, while effects keyed to "unevolved Pokémon" do apply to it
While in play, the four pieces are treated as one combined card; anywhere else — hand, deck, discard pile, or Prizes — each of the four is its own separate card
A deck-searching or similar effect touching individual pieces outside of play can only move one of those separate pieces at a time

Off the combined card, only its type, its Pokémon category, and its card name can be checked on an individual piece — traits like an attack, an Ability, HP, Retreat Cost, Weakness, or Resistance can't be checked on a lone piece
While assembled and in play, still counts as both a Pokémon V and a Pokémon with a Rule Box, so a Stadium that strips Abilities from Rule Box Pokémon reaches it too

An individual piece sitting outside of play — in hand, in the deck, or in the discard pile — is not considered a Pokémon with a Rule Box, so effects that search for or target a non-Rule-Box Pokémon can still find it there
tcg-Appendix 10: Pokémon V-UNION.summary: A Pokémon V-UNION is assembled from four same-named pieces that must enter play together from the discard pile as a single giant card, but count as four separate cards everywhere else and carry their own tight web of exceptions.

terms.meaning: A Battle Style label for cards built around forceful, hard-hitting attacks.
A Battle Style label for cards built around quick, technical attacks.
A Battle Style label for cards that blend the Single Strike and Rapid Strike approaches through teamwork.
Trainer cards and Energy cards can also carry a Battle Style label, typically supporting Pokémon that share that same style.
terms.term: Battle Style tag on Trainer and Energy cards

state: Always printed as a Basic Pokémon
tcg-Appendix 12: Pokémon V.summary: Pokémon V are Basic Pokémon built around large HP totals and hard-hitting attacks, balanced by a bigger payout for the opponent if one falls.

state: Is a new Evolution stage and follows the ordinary rules for evolving
Evolves only from the matching-named Pokémon V beneath it, not from a plain Pokémon of that name
Still counts as a Pokémon V for any effect that references Pokémon V
tcg-Appendix 13: Pokémon VMAX.summary: Pokémon VMAX push a Pokémon V to an even larger scale — commonly 300 or more HP — which makes the opponent's payoff for a Knock Out steeper in turn.

state: The region word (such as a Paldean, Hisuian, Galarian, or Alolan tag) is part of the card's name, not a separate marker
Evolves only from a lower stage sharing that same regional tag, never from the plain version or from a different region's version
Because the names differ, a deck can hold a full legal count of both the regional and the original version of the same species
tcg-Appendix 14: Regional Variants.summary: A regional variant carries its region as part of its card name, which both keeps it distinct from the original Pokémon for deck-building and narrows down exactly which lower stage it can evolve from.

state: Discarding additional cards when the card is played unlocks a further bonus effect beyond its printed base effect
Each TAG TEAM Supporter's effect and bonus are unique to that card
tcg-Appendix 15: TAG TEAM Supporter Card.summary: A TAG TEAM Supporter pairs two Trainers on a single Supporter card and rewards discarding extra cards on play with an added bonus effect layered on top of its own unique base effect.

state: Its GX attack can gain a bonus when a printed requirement is met, such as attaching extra Energy or playing a particular Trainer card
tcg-Appendix 16: TAG TEAM.summary: A TAG TEAM is a Basic Pokémon-GX built from multiple Pokémon joining together, trading a heavier Knock-Out payout for large HP and a GX attack that grows under the right conditions.

state: Limited to a single copy of any given Prism Star name, though different Prism Star names may each appear once in the same deck
A Prism Star card that would be discarded is sent to the Lost Zone instead
tcg-Appendix 17: Prism Star Cards.summary: Prism Star cards, marked with their own symbol, cap each distinctly-named Prism Star card at one copy, but that limit is per name rather than per deck, so several different Prism Star names can sit in the same deck together.

state: Rare Fossil, Unidentified Fossil and any Fossil card with “Antique” in its name are Item cards playable as a Basic Pokémon
Each can evolve into any printed Fossil Pokémon whose card text names that same Rare Fossil or Unidentified Fossil as its origin
A Fossil card with "Antique" in its name instead evolves only into the one specific Pokémon its own printed text identifies
tcg-Appendix 18: Rare Fossil, Unidentifi.summary: Rare Fossil, Unidentified Fossil and Antique Fossil cards are Item cards that can be played as Basic Pokémon. The first two evolve into any matching Fossil Pokémon; an Antique Fossil evolves into whichever single Pokémon its own text names.

state: A GX attack can be used at most once per game, pooled across every Pokémon-GX a player controls
The GX marker is turned face down once that one-time attack has been used, to record the allowance as spent
tcg-Appendix 19: Pokémon-GX.summary: Pokémon-GX combine extra HP and stronger attacks with a single powerful GX attack that can be unleashed only once across an entire game, however many Pokémon-GX a player has in play.

effects.Deck building: no dedicated cap beyond the usual name-based copy limit

state: Treated as a Pokémon ex for any card effect that references Pokémon ex
Can be printed as a Basic, a Stage 1, or a Stage 2 card
Carries none of the extra restrictions the older Mega Evolution Pokémon-EX did — nothing about putting one into play ends your turn
A few sit off the usual ladder — one enters play as a Basic outright, and others attach a stage or two earlier in their family than their name suggests
Only evolves from the exact stage its own card specifies, never from an unrelated stage of the same-named line
tcg-Appendix 1: Mega Evolution Pokémon e.summary: Mega Evolution Pokémon ex push Pokémon ex even further with higher HP and stronger attacks, at the cost of surrendering 3 Prize cards on a Knock Out; beyond that steeper cost, they follow ordinary deck-building and Evolution rules.

state: Identified by a bar in the card's upper-right corner
Some cards carry effects that single out Ultra Beasts specifically
Every Ultra Beast has at least one attack tied to Prize cards
tcg-Appendix 20: Ultra Beasts.summary: Ultra Beasts show up as Pokémon-GX with a crimson color scheme instead of the usual GX blue, and every one of them packs an attack that interacts with Prize cards in some way.

state: Affected by card effects tied to either of its two types
When it attacks, damage is adjusted if the defending Pokémon has a Weakness or Resistance to either of the attacker's two types
Where the defender is Weak to one of those types and Resistant to the other, apply the Weakness first and the Resistance second
tcg-Appendix 21: Dual-Type Pokémon.summary: A dual-type Pokémon holds two types at once, so any card effect keyed to either type reaches it, and either type can trigger a defender's Weakness or Resistance when it attacks.

state: Keeps every attack and Ability the stage beneath it had
Keeps that same stage's Weakness, Resistance, and Retreat Cost
May add further attacks or Abilities, change its HP, and even change type on top of what it inherited
tcg-Appendix 22: BREAK Evolution.summary: A Pokémon BREAK folds forward everything its prior stage could do, then piles extra capability on top of it.

state: Printed directly under the Pokémon's name rather than in the attack or Ability text box
Neither an attack nor an Ability, so card effects that block or remove attacks or Abilities don't reach it
tcg-Appendix 23: Ancient Traits.summary: An Ancient Trait is a special power printed just beneath a Pokémon's name that sits outside both the attack and Ability categories, so effects that shut down attacks or Abilities leave it untouched.

state: Are Pokémon Tool cards attached to an opponent's Pokémon-EX
Produce a negative effect on the Pokémon they're attached to
If removed from that Pokémon for any reason, go to the discard pile belonging to whichever player originally played the card, not the Pokémon's owner
tcg-Appendix 24: Team Flare Hyper Gear.summary: Team Flare Hyper Gear cards are Pokémon Tools meant to be attached to an opponent's Pokémon-EX to work against it, and they land back in whoever played them's discard pile if they're ever removed.

tcg-Appendix 25: Pokémon-EX.summary: Pokémon-EX push HP and attack strength above an ordinary Pokémon's, trading that power for extra risk when one falls in battle.

see_also: tcg-Special rules for Mega Evolution Pokémon-EX
tcg-Appendix 26: Mega Evolution Pokémon-.summary: A Mega Evolution Pokémon-EX takes a Pokémon-EX to a further, more powerful peak, so timing when to bring one into play matters as much as the card itself.

state: Recognizable by a shared visual treatment across Pokémon, Trainer, and Energy cards carrying the label
For a Pokémon card, the Team Plasma label is not part of the card's name, so it counts toward the same name-based copy limit as the non-Team-Plasma version
Evolves the same way an ordinary Pokémon of that line would
tcg-Appendix 27: Team Plasma Cards.summary: Team Plasma cards are identifiable by a distinctive look, but unlike other named variants the Team Plasma label is not part of a Pokémon's card name, so it shares its copy limit with the plain version rather than getting its own.

state: Enters the Bench only through the effect of its own printed matching Fossil Item card, not by being played from hand directly
Once in play, a further stage evolves from it the same way any Stage 1 would evolve from its Basic
tcg-Appendix 28: Restored Pokémon.summary: Certain Fossil Pokémon occupy their own unique stage, Restored Pokémon, and only reach the Bench through the effect of their own matching Fossil Item card; once there, later stages evolve from them as usual.

state: The Trainer's name is part of the card's own name, not a separate label
Because the name differs, it evolves only from a lower stage carrying the same Trainer's name — never from the plain, unowned Pokémon
tcg-Appendix 2: Trainer’s Pokémon.summary: A Trainer's Pokémon folds a Trainer's name into its own card name, making it a separate name from the unowned version and confining its Evolution line to cards that share that same ownership.

effects.Deck cap: 1 ACE SPEC card total per deck, combined across every name

state: The cap counts every ACE SPEC card together, regardless of which one it is
tcg-Appendix 3: ACE SPEC Cards.summary: ACE SPEC cards hit hard enough that a deck is limited to a single ACE SPEC card overall, not a single copy of every ACE SPEC name it contains.

terms.meaning: A card label introduced alongside the Paradox Rift era, marking a leaning toward blunt, heavy-hitting attacks.
A card label from the same era as Ancient, marking a leaning toward precise, technical attacks.

state: "ex" is part of the card's name, separate from the non-ex version and from the differently-suffixed Pokémon-EX line
Because all three names differ, a deck can carry a full legal count of each one side by side
tcg-Appendix 5: Pokémon ex.summary: Pokémon ex trade a Knock-Out risk for bigger HP and stronger attacks than an ordinary Pokémon of the same name, and the ex suffix keeps its name distinct from both the plain version and from Pokémon-EX.

state: Immune to attack damage while on the Bench, from either player's attacks
tcg-Appendix 6: Tera Pokémon ex.summary: Tera Pokémon ex shrug off attack damage entirely while parked on the Bench, a protection that holds against both players' attacks; otherwise they carry the same 2-Prize Knock-Out risk as any Pokémon ex.

state: Reachable through attack effects, Ability effects, or Trainer card effects
Unlike the discard pile, cards placed here are permanently unplayable for the remainder of the game
tcg-Appendix 7: Lost Zone.summary: The Lost Zone holds cards that have left the game entirely; attacks, Abilities, and Trainer cards can all route cards there, and nothing that lands in it can come back or be played again for the rest of that game.

state: "Radiant" is part of the card's name, so it's counted separately from a same-species non-Radiant card for deck-building purposes
Always printed as a Basic Pokémon card
Never evolves into anything and is never itself an evolution
Counts as a Pokémon with a Rule Box
tcg-Appendix 8: Radiant Pokémon.summary: Radiant Pokémon show off Shiny coloring and a built-in rule capping a deck at a single Radiant Pokémon; each one is always a standalone Basic that neither evolves nor is evolved from.

state: A VSTAR Power is usable at most once across the entire game, pooled across every Pokémon VSTAR a player controls
Flip the VSTAR marker face down after the power is used, to record that the allowance is gone
Is a new Evolution stage in its own right and follows the ordinary rules for evolving
Evolves only from the matching-named Pokémon V beneath it, not from a plain Pokémon of that name
Still counts as a Pokémon V for any effect that references Pokémon V
tcg-Appendix 9: Pokémon VSTAR.summary: Pokémon VSTAR add a single game-changing VSTAR Power — an Ability or an attack — that can fire only once per game no matter how many Pokémon VSTAR are in play, tracked by flipping a marker once it's spent.

options.detail: Flip again at the next Checkup.

state: Rotated counterclockwise
No attacking
No retreating
tcg-Asleep.summary: A sleeping Pokémon is rotated counterclockwise and skips both attacking and retreating until a coin flip wakes it.

paragraphs: This rulebook covers everything needed to play the Pokémon Trading Card Game, where a 60-card deck stands in for a trainer's Pokémon and the gear that supports them.
It's a strategy game built on collectible cards, so no two decks play quite alike. A preconstructed deck bundled with a strategy sheet is an easy on-ramp for a first game.
From there, growing a collection through booster packs, trading for favorites, and assembling a personal 60-card deck is the path to making the game your own.
tcg-Become a Pokémon Master!.summary: A framing introduction: this rulebook teaches the Pokémon TCG, from a first preconstructed deck through building and trading for a personal 60-card collection.

options.outcome: Add 2 damage counters to the Burned Pokémon

state: Carries a Burn marker (keep it visually distinct from damage counters)
A second burn never stacks — the newer one replaces the older
tcg-Burned.summary: A Burn marker deals two damage counters every Checkup, with a coin flip deciding whether the burn heals.

options.detail: Add 3 damage counters to the Confused Pokémon.

state: Rotated with the card top facing its owner
tcg-Confused.summary: A confused Pokémon is rotated top-toward-you and must win a coin flip to attack; failing hurts it instead.

tcg-Credits.skip: Publication colophon: studio credits, support contacts, trademark notices. No rules content; nothing a player or judge searches for.

see_also: tcg-What does and doesn’t count for a Pokémon’s name?

steps.action: Build to exactly 60 cards.
steps.note: not 59, not 61

steps.action: Cap any single card name at 4 copies.
steps.note: Basic Energy cards are exempt from this cap

steps.action: Include at least one Basic Pokémon.
Settle on one or two Energy types for the deck.
steps.note: most Pokémon can use any Energy type to attack, so a narrow Energy base still fits a wide range of Pokémon

steps.action: Budget roughly 12 to 15 Energy cards.
Budget roughly 20 to 25 Trainer cards.
steps.note: cards that search or draw help find exactly what's needed

steps.action: Fill the rest with Pokémon.
steps.note: aiming for 4 copies of favorites, and 4 of each stage in their Evolution line, keeps them showing up reliably

tcg-Deck Building.summary: Every deck must land on exactly 60 cards, cap any one card name at 4 copies (Basic Energy excepted), and carry at least one Basic Pokémon; from there, a starter split of one or two Energy types, 12-15 Energy, 20-25 Trainers, and Pokémon filling the rest is a reasonable template to adjust from.

terms.meaning: Leans toward attacks that heal the user or Poison the opponent.
Hits hard, can inflict Burned, but its big attacks often need a turn to recharge.
Good at manipulating Energy and shuffling Pokémon between the Active Spot and Bench.
Can recover used Energy back out of the discard pile and can inflict Paralyzed.
Specializes in unusual powers, and tends to inflict Asleep, Confused, or Poisoned on opponents.
Trades risk for reward — extra damage, and some attacks flip coins for bonus hits.
Sneaky attacks that often force the opponent to discard cards, and can inflict Poisoned.
Built to resist incoming attacks longer than most other types.

Dulls the effectiveness of an opponent's attacks. No card of this type is printed in the current Mega Evolution Series, though older expansions do have them, and some cards that once carried it now print as Psychic instead.
Very strong attacks that usually demand two different Energy types to pay for.
Broad movesets that fit into almost any deck, of any type.

steps.action: Confirm the right Energy is attached for the attack you're choosing, then announce it.
Check for any standing effect that could alter or cancel the attack.
steps.note: for example, a lingering effect from an attack used against you last turn; such effects vanish the moment the affected Pokémon leaves the Active Spot for the Bench, so a Pokémon swapped in since then is unaffected

steps.action: If the attacking Pokémon is Confused, resolve that coin flip now before anything else.
Make any choice the attack requires, such as picking a target.
Carry out anything the attack demands to be used, such as a required coin flip.
Resolve any effects timed to happen before damage, deal the damage, then resolve every remaining effect.
Start from the attack's printed base damage.
steps.note: a ×, +, or – symbol next to that number means the attack text spells out the adjustment; if the attack instead instructs placing damage counters directly, stop here and place them — counters placed that way skip Weakness, Resistance, and every other damage modifier

steps.action: Work out any damage adjustment on the attacking Pokémon, up or down, from a Trainer card or any other effect in force.
steps.note: a lingering effect from one of its own earlier attacks is the common case; skip this and every remaining damage step if the base damage is 0 or the attack deals no damage at all

steps.action: Multiply for Weakness if the target has Weakness to the attacker's type.
Subtract for Resistance if the target has Resistance to the attacker's type.
Apply any remaining damage-changing effect on the target from a Trainer card, Energy card, or similar source.
Convert the final total into damage counters, one per 10 points.
steps.note: a final total of 0 or less places no damage counters

tcg-Full details of attacking.summary: Most attacks are simple in practice, but the full sequence runs from announcing the attack through standing effects, Confusion, required choices, and a fixed damage-math order ending in placed damage counters.

steps.action: Both hands empty of Basics? Show them, reshuffle, and restart setup together
One player only: they declare the mulligan and wait for the opponent to finish setting up
The stuck player shows their hand, shuffles it into their deck, and redraws until a Basic appears
The other player may then draw one card per extra mulligan taken beyond their own count
steps.note: example: 2 mulligans each plus 3 extra by one side lets the other side draw up to 3; any Basics drawn this way may go straight to the Bench

steps.action: Reveal all Active and Benched Pokémon and start the game

tcg-Full details of taking a mulligan.summary: A hand with zero Basic Pokémon gets shuffled away and redrawn, and the opponent may profit with bonus draws.

terms.meaning: A non-attack effect printed on a Pokémon; some run constantly, others must be activated — read each one for its exact timing.
A high-power card class capped at a single copy per deck.
Your one in-play Pokémon that isn't Benched; only it can attack.
A special power printed under certain Pokémon's names; neither attack nor Ability, so effects that shut those off leave it alone.
Moving a card from hand onto one of your in-play Pokémon.
Either the act of your Active Pokémon fighting, or the printed move text on a card — a Pokémon may carry several.
The Active Pokémon while it performs an attack.
An Energy card of one of the nine basic types: Grass, Fire, Water, Lightning, Psychic, Fighting, Darkness, Metal, or Fairy.
A Pokémon playable straight from your hand on your turn.
Home for in-play Pokémon not currently fighting; they step in when the Active retreats or is Knocked Out, and ignore Weakness and Resistance while Benched.
Older name for Pokémon Checkup — the hand-off point between turns where conditions resolve and Knock Outs are checked.
An Evolution that keeps every attack, Ability, Weakness, Resistance, and Retreat Cost of the stage beneath it.
The reminder marker for Burned; comes off when the Pokémon benches or evolves.
The usual product of an attack; reaching total damage at or above Hit Points means a Knock Out.
A marker representing 10 damage that persists through benching and evolving; 50s and 100s are shorthand only — rules text always means the 10 unit.
The Pokémon on the receiving end of an attack.
Undoing an evolution; the devolved Pokémon also sheds Special Conditions and lingering effects.
Your face-up discards, open for anyone to inspect at any time.
A Pokémon holding two types simultaneously.
Fuel for attacks; see Basic Energy card.
Played on top of a Basic (or a lower Evolution) to power it up.
An in-play Pokémon stacked on top of another.
Trainer cards that behave like Basic Pokémon once in play — but count as Trainers, not Basics, while in hand, deck, or discard.
A once-per-game super attack exclusive to Pokémon-GX.
A reminder token flipped face down once your game's GX attack is spent.
The damage budget a Pokémon can absorb before being Knocked Out.
On the table: your board Pokémon and attachments. Deck, discard pile, and Prizes don't count; the Bench does.
A Trainer card you resolve and discard.
Damage at or past Hit Points sends the Pokémon and its attachments to the discard pile — and hands your opponent a Prize.
Exile: cards there are out of the game, kept face up beside play.
A Pokémon ex upgrade that surrenders 3 Prizes when Knocked Out.
A Pokémon-EX upgrade; forming one ends your turn.
The reminder marker for Poisoned; comes off when the Pokémon benches or evolves.
An always-on effect lasting while its Pokémon is in play.
A once-per-turn optional power, usually disabled while its Pokémon has a Special Condition.
The game's fighters, represented by Basic Pokémon and Evolution cards.
The current name for the between-turns step: resolve Poisoned, Burned, Asleep, and Paralyzed, then check for Knock Outs.
Powerful, but worth 2 Prizes when Knocked Out; distinct from Pokémon-EX.
A stronger form worth two Prizes when Knocked Out; distinct from Pokémon ex.
A stronger form worth two Prizes when Knocked Out, each packing a GX attack.
Twin cards depicting Legendary Pokémon, playable only as a pair.
An upgrade placed on the same-named Pokémon, adding capabilities.
Legacy umbrella for Poké-Power and Poké-Body, always labeled as such.
A Pokémon bearing an ownership mark in its name; the mark makes it a different name from the plain version.
A Trainer card attached to a Pokémon, one Tool per Pokémon.
High-HP Basics with strong attacks, worth 2 Prizes when Knocked Out.
The next stage of Pokémon V — enormous HP, worth 3 Prizes when Knocked Out.
Evolves from Pokémon V, worth 2 Prizes when Knocked Out, each with a VSTAR Power.
A four-card giant assembled onto the Bench from the discard pile, all pieces at once.
Limited to one of each name per deck, and heads to the Lost Zone instead of the discard pile.
Your six face-down setup cards; each opposing Knock Out pays out one (or more for premium Pokémon), and the last one wins you the game.
A Shiny-colored Basic, capped at one per deck.
Reduced damage from attackers of a listed type.
Played via its matching fossil Item card.
Swapping the Active for a Benched Pokémon at the cost of discarding Energy equal to Retreat Cost — once per turn.
The five afflictions: Asleep, Burned, Confused, Paralyzed, Poisoned.
A Trainer that stays on the table; only one Stadium at a time (a newcomer discards the old), one played per turn.
A Trainer limited to one per turn.
A Basic Pokémon-GX pairing with a 3-Prize penalty and a bonus-boosted GX attack.
Two Trainers sharing one Supporter; discard extra cards on play to unlock its bonus.
A Trainer attached to a Pokémon, lending it the printed attack while attached.
A Pokémon ex shielded from attack damage while Benched; still worth 2 Prizes.
When both players win simultaneously, a fresh game decides it — first Prize taken wins.
The advantage-generating card family: Items, Tools, Stadiums, Supporters.
A Pokémon whose title carries its Trainer's name; ownership is part of the name, so it only evolves within the same owned line.
A reminder token flipped face down once your game's VSTAR Power is spent.
A once-per-game attack or Ability exclusive to Pokémon VSTAR.
Increased damage from attackers of a listed type.

state: You win by taking your final Prize card
You win if your opponent has no Pokémon remaining in play
You win if your opponent cannot draw a card at the start of their turn
tcg-How to Win.summary: Three roads to victory: collect all your Prizes, empty the opponent's board, or leave them unable to draw.

state: Claiming your final Prize card wins the game outright.
Clearing every one of your opponent's Pokémon from play wins the game outright.
An opponent unable to draw a card at the start of their own turn loses the game.
tcg-How to Win the Game.summary: Three routes to victory: collect every Prize card, wipe out the opponent's Pokémon in play, or leave them stuck with an empty deck on their draw step.

state: Cannot be moved from hand to the Bench except through an Item card whose effect specifically allows it
Is not a Basic Pokémon, so it cannot be the starting Active or Benched Pokémon during setup
A deck made up only of Restored Pokémon still needs at least one ordinary Basic Pokémon
Is not an Evolution card in its own right
Card effects keyed to "Basic," "Stage 1," "Stage 2," or "Evolution" skip over it, though effects that simply reference "a Pokémon" or "unevolved Pokémon" still reach it

Which further stage it can evolve into is governed entirely by the "Evolves from" or "put this card into play" text printed on the cards actually in play, so an older or newer printing of the same Fossil family can still link up across stages as long as that printed text matches
tcg-Key Restored Pokémon Notes.summary: Restored Pokémon carry a cluster of exceptions: they reach the Bench only through their matching Item card, don't count as Basic or Evolution cards for other effects, and evolve according to whatever "Evolves from" text is printed on the specific cards in play.

state: An Ability or Trainer card effect written to happen 'during Pokémon Checkup' or 'between turns' resolves at that step.

The player about to take the next turn decides where that effect falls relative to the Special Conditions, but the Special Conditions themselves always resolve back-to-back as one uninterrupted block — an effect can go before the block, after it, or both, never inserted partway through.
tcg-Other Effects.summary: Any Ability or Trainer effect that names Pokémon Checkup (or 'between turns') as its trigger — for instance, one that heals a small amount of damage each turn — resolves during that step, bookending the Special Conditions block rather than splitting it.

ends_when: The Checkup after its owner's next turn ends — stand the card back up
state: Rotated clockwise
No attacking
No retreating
tcg-Paralyzed.summary: A paralyzed Pokémon is rotated clockwise and frozen out of attacking and retreating for one round.

tcg-Parts of a Pokémon Card.skip: Diagram callout labels only — no prose in the source, so any entry would be invented rather than authored. Card anatomy is not searchable rules content.

steps.action: Draw a card.
Take any of the following actions in whatever order you like, repeating any of them as often as their own limit allows
steps.note: benching Basic Pokémon and evolving have no turn limit; attaching Energy and retreating are capped at once each; Trainer cards are unlimited except for one Supporter and one Stadium per turn; Abilities have no turn limit

steps.action: Attack, which immediately ends your turn.

tcg-Parts of a Turn.summary: A turn breaks into three parts: draw a card, take any mix of the turn's optional actions, then attack to close it out.

paragraphs: This covers everything needed to start playing. For more hands-on help, a local hobby store can point to a League Battle Deck — a preconstructed deck bundled with gameplay advice, ready to play out of the box.
Official Play! Pokémon stores also run organized play: a chance to learn the game, battle other players, and earn prizes along the way. Any hobby store can say whether it holds that status.
tcg-Play! Pokémon Stores and League Batt.summary: Closing pointer: a local hobby store's League Battle Deck and Play! Pokémon organized-play program are the next steps after this rulebook.

paragraphs: The Pokémon TCG plays fast — this section is the quick-start summary for getting a game going right away.
tcg-Playing the Game.summary: A one-line framing note introducing the quick-start summary that follows.

options.outcome: Add 1 damage counter to the Poisoned Pokémon

state: Carries a Poison marker (keep it visually distinct from damage counters)
A second poisoning never stacks — the newer one replaces the older
tcg-Poisoned.summary: A Poison marker drips one damage counter at every Checkup and stays until the Pokémon benches, evolves, or is healed.

state: Evolving or returning to the Bench cures every Special Condition at once
Retreating is blocked only by Asleep and Paralyzed
Asleep, Confused, and Paralyzed share the card rotation — the newest of the three is the only one in effect
Burned and Poisoned live on markers, so they coexist with the rotation conditions
A single Pokémon can suffer Burned, Paralyzed, and Poisoned simultaneously
tcg-Removing Special Conditions.summary: Benching or evolving clears everything; rotations overwrite each other while markers stack independently.

see_also: tcg-Full details of taking a mulligan

steps.action: Greet your opponent with a handshake
Coin flip
steps.note: the winner picks who takes the first turn

steps.action: Shuffle your 60 cards and draw 7
Look for Basic Pokémon among your 7
steps.note: none at all? See the mulligan rules

steps.action: Choose one Basic as your Active Pokémon, placed face down
Add up to 5 more Basics face down to your Bench
Deal yourself 6 face-down Prize cards from the top of your deck
Both players turn their Pokémon face up and begin

tcg-Setting Up to Play.summary: Eight steps take both players from handshake to a face-down board ready to reveal.

state: Only the Active Pokémon can have a Special Condition
Moving to the Bench removes every Special Condition
Evolving removes every Special Condition
tcg-Special Conditions.summary: Five Special Conditions can afflict the Active Pokémon: Asleep, Burned, Confused, Paralyzed, and Poisoned.

state: The Mega marker is part of the card's name, separate from the base Pokémon-EX, so a deck can carry a full legal count of both
Evolves only from the matching-named Pokémon-EX, never from the plain, unevolved Pokémon
Occupies its own new stage and counts as an Evolution card, following the ordinary rules for evolving
Turning one of your Pokémon into a Mega Evolution Pokémon-EX ends your turn immediately, so any other actions need to happen first
A Primal Reversion Pokémon-EX is governed by this same set of rules
tcg-Special rules for Mega Evolution Pok.summary: A Mega Evolution Pokémon-EX's name carries its own Mega marker, it can only evolve from the matching Pokémon-EX beneath it, it still counts as a Pokémon-EX for the Knock-Out payout, and putting one into play immediately ends the turn.

state: "BREAK" is part of the card's name, separate from the pre-BREAK version, so a deck can carry a full legal count of both
Occupies its own new stage, counts as an Evolution card, and follows the ordinary rules for evolving
tcg-Special rules for Pokémon BREAK.summary: BREAK is folded into a Pokémon BREAK's own card name, and BREAK forms its own Evolution stage that plays by the standard Evolution rules.

state: "EX" is part of the card's name, separate from the non-EX version, so a deck can carry a full legal count of both
Otherwise handled exactly like any other Pokémon card during play

tcg-Special rules for Pokémon-EX.summary: The EX suffix keeps a Pokémon-EX's name distinct from its plain counterpart, it plays exactly like any other Pokémon card apart from that, and it comes with a steeper Knock-Out cost.

state: "GX" is part of the card's name, separate from the non-GX version, so a deck can carry a full legal count of both
When evolving from a shared lower stage, the player may choose either the non-GX or the GX result
Follows the same Evolution stages and rules as an ordinary Pokémon, including being playable as a starting Active Pokémon when it's a Basic
tcg-Special rules for Pokémon-GX.summary: The GX suffix keeps a Pokémon-GX's name distinct from its non-GX counterpart, either can be chosen when evolving from the shared lower stage, and losing one gives the opponent a bigger Prize payout than an ordinary Pokémon.

steps.action: Draw a card from the top of your deck to open your turn.
steps.note: an empty deck when your turn begins means you lose immediately

steps.action: Move Basic Pokémon from your hand onto your Bench, face up.
steps.note: as many as you want, up to a 5-Pokémon Bench

steps.action: Evolve Pokémon already in play by placing the next stage on top of them, Active or Benched alike.
steps.note: as many as you want; the Pokémon keeps its attachments and damage counters but sheds Special Conditions and attack effects; once evolved it can no longer reach down for whatever attacks or Abilities were printed on the card underneath, unless something explicitly grants that; a Pokémon can't evolve on the very turn it enters play — that rules out evolving a Basic the same turn it's benched, on any turn of the game, and it also rules out evolving the same Pokémon twice in one turn, since evolving counts as entering play again; separately, neither player may evolve anything at all on their own first turn of the game unless a card overrides that

steps.action: Attach one Energy card from your hand to a Pokémon of your choice.
steps.note: limited to a single attachment per turn

steps.action: Play Trainer cards and resolve their printed rule.
steps.note: Items and Pokémon Tools have no turn limit; only one Supporter and one Stadium may be played per turn; a newly played Stadium replaces and discards whichever one was already in play, and a same-named Stadium can't be played over itself; the player taking the game's first turn may not play a Supporter that turn

steps.action: Retreat your Active Pokémon, discarding Energy equal to its Retreat Cost, and bring up a Benched Pokémon in its place.
steps.note: once per turn; damage counters and attachments travel with each Pokémon; blocked while the Active Pokémon is Asleep or Paralyzed; attacking afterward with the new Active Pokémon is still allowed

steps.action: Use any Abilities you want, on Pokémon Active or Benched.
steps.note: say out loud which ones you are using so your opponent can follow; using an Ability isn't an attack, so it doesn't cost you your attack for the turn

steps.action: Choose whether to attack with your Active Pokémon.
steps.note: ending the turn either way; the player going first skips this on the game's opening turn

steps.action: Resolve Pokémon Checkup before the next player's turn begins.
steps.note: Special Conditions are always applied in a fixed order — Poisoned, then Burned, then Asleep, then Paralyzed — and once that block starts it runs straight through with nothing inserted partway; the player about to take the next turn chooses where any Ability or Trainer effect timed to this step falls relative to that block (before it, after it, or bookending both sides), just never in the middle of it; any Pokémon left with no HP is Knocked Out and replaced before play continues

tcg-Turn Actions.summary: The full turn-action menu: draw, then freely mix benching, evolving, one Energy attachment, Trainer plays, one retreat, and Abilities, then attack and hand off through Pokémon Checkup.

state: A move counts as an attack if it carries a cost and a name, whether or not it deals damage.
Anything printed as an Ability, or labeled some other way, is not an attack even if it produces a similar effect.
Effects that specifically key off 'attacks' apply only to genuine attacks, never to Abilities or other non-attack effects.
tcg-What counts as an attack?.summary: Any move with a printed cost and name is an attack, damage or not — everything else, such as an Ability, is not, even when it does something similar.

effects.A Delta Species marking: Not part of the name — shares its name with the non-Delta version
effects.A Level marking on a Pokémon card: Not part of the name — every Level of that Pokémon shares one name
effects.A trailing symbol on a Pokémon card: Part of the name — a card with the symbol has a different name from the plain version
effects.An owner's name or a regional/form label: Part of the name — distinct from the unlabeled version

state: A deck may hold only 4 cards sharing one full name, Basic Energy cards excepted; names that differ under these rules each get their own 4-card allowance.
Evolving requires the printed 'Evolves from' name to match the in-play Pokémon's exact name — a Level difference doesn't block the match, but an owner or form label does.
tcg-What does and doesn’t count for a Po.summary: Levels and Delta Species markings don't change a Pokémon's name, but trailing symbols and owner or form labels do — and that distinction drives both the 4-copy deck limit and whether a card evolves from a given Pokémon.

options.condition: One player satisfies both win conditions while the other satisfies only one
options.outcome: The player meeting both conditions wins outright

options.condition: Neither player has the edge described above

branch.when: Both players satisfy a win condition simultaneously

state: Taking your last Prize card wins the game.
An opponent left with an empty Bench when their Active Pokémon is Knocked Out or otherwise removed also wins the game for you.
Both conditions can be true for both players in the same moment.
tcg-What if both players win at the same.summary: A shared win moment is possible; whoever satisfies more of the win conditions takes it outright, and a genuine tie goes to a tiebreaker game.

state: Told to draw or look at more cards than remain in your deck, draw or look at whatever is left and continue play normally.
Losing for failing to draw only applies to the mandatory draw at the start of your turn — not to a shortfall caused by a card effect asking you to draw or look at cards.
tcg-What if you should draw more cards t.summary: A card effect asking for more cards than are left in the deck just draws or reveals whatever remains; only an empty deck at the start of your own turn costs you the game.

see_also: tcg-What if both players win at the same time?

steps.action: Set up exactly as for a normal game, including 6 Prize cards for each player.
Flip a coin to decide who takes the first turn.
Play until one player takes a Prize card, or otherwise ends up with fewer Prizes remaining than their opponent.
steps.note: that player wins; every other normal win condition still applies during a tiebreaker

tcg-What’s a tiebreaker game?.summary: A tiebreaker is a fresh full game where the first player to claim a Prize card — or otherwise pull ahead on Prizes remaining — wins the race.

effects.Attack effect phrased 'up to X': Choose any number from 0 to X
effects.Effect phrased 'any amount' or 'any numb: Choose any number from 0 up to the maximum
effects.Non-attack effect phrased 'up to X' (Tra: Choose any number from 1 to X
effects.Unrestricted deck or discard-pile search: Must choose at least 1 card, whether or not the effect is an attack

tcg-What’s the difference between “up to.summary: 'Up to X' allows zero on an attack effect but requires at least one on a non-attack effect, and an 'up to X' search of deck or discard for any card at all requires at least one either way; 'any amount' and 'any number' allow zero.

terms.meaning: Each player's own 60-card pile. Both players can see how many cards remain in either deck, but neither may look at or reorder either deck unless a card permits it.
Cards drawn stay hidden here; a game starts with 7. Opponents may not look at each other's hand unless a card says otherwise.
6 cards each player sets face down from the top of their own deck during setup. Knocking out an opposing Pokémon lets you claim one into your hand; being first to claim your last one wins the game.
The single slot each player must always fill with exactly one Pokémon — the only one that can attack. An opponent with none left to put here loses.
Holds every other in-play Pokémon, up to 5 at a time; anything in play besides the Active Pokémon has to sit here.

Each player's own face-up pile of cards taken out of play, open for either player to inspect at any time; a Knocked Out Pokémon and everything attached to it lands in its owner's pile unless a card says otherwise.
